chief_complaint: episodic severe pain in the right upper stomach that lasts for hours after heavy meals
hpi_details: Presents with a 3-month history of distinct episodes of severe, dull, aching right upper quadrant pain occurring typically 1 to 2 hours after eating rich or creamy food. Pain builds over 30 minutes, plateaus for 2-3 hours, radiates to her right mid-back, and resolves spontaneously without residual ache. Reports three episodes this month. No fever, chills, yellow eyes, or changes in stool colour.
ideas: thinks she might have gallstones like her sister had last year
concerns: worried that an episode will happen while she is driving her children on the motorway
expectations: wants an ultrasound scan and advice on whether she needs gallbladder surgery
pmh: gestational diabetes during third pregnancy 5 years ago, obesity
social_hx: non-smoker, no alcohol intake, mother of three, part-time librarian

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Biliary Colic is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Arrange elective transabdominal ultrasound to confirm cholelithiasis, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: episodic severe pain in the right upper stomach that lasts for hours after heavy meals

Key HPI features: Presents with a 3-month history of distinct episodes of severe, dull, aching right upper quadrant pain occurring typically 1 to 2 hours after eating rich or creamy food. Pain builds over 30 minutes, plateaus for 2-3 hours, radiates to her right mid-back, and resolves spontaneously without residual ache. Reports three episodes this month. No fever, chills, yellow eyes, or changes in stool colour.

Objective/Exam findings: Abdominal exam: completely soft, non-tender in RUQ, negative Murphy's sign (as patient is between attacks). Bloods: LFTs (normal bilirubin/ALP/ALT expected), FBC, amylase. Transabdominal ultrasound scan.
Relevant background/PMH: gestational diabetes during third pregnancy 5 years ago, obesity
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Biliary Colic.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Peptic ulcer disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever or pain lasting beyond several hours without resolving — would suggest cholecystitis rather than simple colic.
management_principles: Arrange elective transabdominal ultrasound to confirm cholelithiasis
Reassure regarding normal interval examination and absence of infection
Provide dietary counseling: low-fat diet to reduce gallbladder contraction triggers
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 44F presents with recurrent episodic 2-3 hr postprandial RUQ pain radiating to right back. Spontaneous complete resolution between attacks. No pyrexia or jaundice.
reference_soap.objective: Abdominal exam: completely soft, non-tender in RUQ, negative Murphy's sign (as patient is between attacks). Bloods: LFTs (normal bilirubin/ALP/ALT expected), FBC, amylase. Transabdominal ultrasound scan.
reference_soap.assessment: Biliary colic due to cholelithiasis without cholecystitis or ductal obstruction. DDx: peptic ulcer disease, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, functional dyspepsia, sphincter of Oddi dysfunction.
reference_soap.plan: Arrange elective transabdominal ultrasound to confirm cholelithiasis. Reassure regarding normal interval examination and absence of infection. Provide dietary counseling: low-fat diet to reduce gallbladder contraction triggers. Analgesia prescription (NSAIDs e.g. diclofenac/ibuprofen or paracetamol PRN for attacks). Refer to general surgery for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

learning_objectives: Differentiate biliary colic from acute cholecystitis based on episodic duration (<6 hours) and complete inter-attack resolution
Recognise the classic biliary pain pattern plateau and crescendo mechanics
Provide evidence-based dietary modifications to minimize cholecystokinin-mediated gallbladder contractions
Outline the pathway for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy and red flags requiring emergency return

teaching.one_liner: A gallstone temporarily blocks the gallbladder outlet after a fatty meal, causing steady right-upper-quadrant pain that builds, plateaus, and then fully resolves.
red_flags: Fever or pain lasting beyond several hours without resolving — would suggest cholecystitis rather than simple colic

must_ask.say: Does the pain start an hour or two after eating rich or fatty food?
Does the pain go away completely on its own after a few hours, without leaving any ache?
Does it spread through to your shoulder blade or the middle of your back?
Have you had any fevers or chills with these episodes?
Have you noticed any yellowing of your skin or eyes, or a change in stool colour?
How many of these episodes have you had, and how often?

history.answer: I've been getting this terrible pain in the upper right side of my stomach after heavy meals, and it lasted for hours each time.
It started about three months ago. Whenever an attack happens, the ache builds up gradually over about thirty minutes.
It is in the upper right part of my belly under my ribs. It stays right there and doesn't move across my stomach.
Yes, when the pain is at its peak, the ache spreads straight through to my right mid-back. It doesn't go to my shoulder or groin.
It is a severe, dull, aching pressure. Once it reaches its peak, it stays constant rather than coming and going in sharp waves.
It gets very severe, about an eight out of ten. The intense ache plateaus for about two to three hours and then resolves completely without any lingering soreness.
It typically comes on an hour or two after eating rich, creamy, or fatty food. Nothing really relieves it during an attack, but between episodes I feel completely normal.
Yes, I've had several similar episodes over the past three months. I've had three bad attacks just this month alone.
I feel somewhat nauseous when the pain is worst, but I haven't thrown up. There has been no vomiting of bile or blood.
My bowels have been moving normally every day. I haven't had any diarrhea, constipation, or pale clay-coloured stools.
No, I haven't had any fever, night sweats, or chills at all.
No, my eyes and skin haven't turned yellow, and my urine hasn't looked unusually dark or tea-coloured.
No burning with urination, no blood in my urine, and no need to pee more often.
No, I haven't experienced any dizziness, lightheadedness, or blackouts.
No abnormal spotting, unusual vaginal bleeding, or discharge.
No chest tightness, heart palpitations, or shortness of breath.
My last attack happened about an hour and a half after a rich, creamy pasta dinner. I don't drink any alcohol.
No, I don't take aspirin or regular anti-inflammatory painkillers.
No, I don't have any heart rhythm problems, clots, or blood vessel conditions.
I was wondering if this could be gallstones. My sister had gallstones last year and her attacks sounded very similar to mine.
I'm terrified that one of these severe attacks will strike while I'm driving my children on the motorway.
I would like to get an ultrasound scan of my abdomen and find out if I need surgery to remove my gallbladder.
I had gestational diabetes when I was pregnant with my third child five years ago, and I struggle with being overweight.
I haven't had any operations. My only hospital stays were for the births of my three children.
I only take an over-the-counter multivitamin once a day.
No, I don't have any allergies to medications.
I have never smoked.
I don't drink any alcohol at all.
I work part-time as a librarian, and I live with my husband and our three children.
My sister had gallstones and had her gallbladder removed last year, but there are no other significant illnesses in my family.
My last period was about two weeks ago and my cycles are regular. There is no chance that I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Sclerae are clear and anicteric; conjunctivae are pink without pallor.
Abdomen is mildly obese, symmetrical, and non-distended, with no surgical scars, distended veins, or visible masses.
Normoactive bowel sounds present in all four quadrants with no audible bruits.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender throughout; no tenderness, guarding, or palpable masses in the right upper quadrant or elsewhere.
No rebound tenderness or involuntary abdominal rigidity in any quadrant.
Negative Murphy's sign without inspiratory arrest during deep palpation of the right subcostal margin.
No tenderness at McBurney's point, and psoas and obturator signs are negative.
Normal sphincter tone with no rectal mass or tenderness, and normal brown stool on the glove without blood.
